name: Survival / Crafting
description: Survive, gather, craft and build in a hostile world, on top of a simulated world with weather and a day/night cycle.

pillars.name: Scarcity Drives Decisions
pillars.rulesOut: infinite supplies, needs that never pressure

pillars.name: Build Your Haven
pillars.feeling: the base I made is home

gameExamples.heading: Pitch
gameExamples.text: A survival game set in a frozen wilderness where the player scavenges, crafts and builds a shelter to outlast the winter.

gameExamples.heading: Core Loop
gameExamples.text:
1. Venture out to gather.
2. Survive the cold and the creatures.
3. Return to base and craft.
4. Build up the base and prepare for night.

docs.title: Survival Needs
docs.summary: Health, hunger, thirst, temperature and how they pressure the player.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can keep my character fed, warm and healthy.
- As a player, I can see which need is most urgent.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Need meters that flash when low.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Needs drain slowly but never stop.
- No need kills instantly.

docs.title: Needs System
docs.summary: How needs tick, interact and are saved.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Each need is a value that drains over time; modifiers (shelter, clothing, weather) change the drain rate.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UNeedsComponent`: need values and drain
- `UNeedModifier`: a change to drain rates

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Drain rates in a data asset.

docs.title: Gathering
docs.summary: Collecting resources from the world: tools, nodes and yields.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can gather resources with tools.
- As a player, I can see how much a node has left.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Nodes that visibly deplete.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Better tools gather faster.
- Nodes regrow after a few days.

docs.title: Crafting
docs.summary: Turning resources into tools, gear and supplies.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can combine materials into items.
- As a player, I can see which recipes I can make right now.
- As a player, I can queue several crafts.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A recipe list with missing materials highlighted.
- A progress bar for each craft.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Some recipes need a station.
- Crafting can't be cancelled after it finishes.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.summary: What can be made, and how the player discovers it.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can discover recipes by finding materials.
- As a player, I can see what a recipe needs.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - New recipes announced when unlocked.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - Recipes unlock when the player picks up a needed material.

docs.title: Crafting System
docs.summary: Recipe data, stations and crafting queues.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Recipes are data assets; crafting stations have queues that consume inputs and produce outputs over time.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UCraftingComponent`: queues and timers
- `URecipeData`: inputs, outputs, station and time

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Recipes as data assets.

docs.summary: Tool, gear and supply meshes and icons.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Item meshes | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Item icons | UI | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Items read clearly at icon size; rarity is shown through color and glow, not detail.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Item packs that include both meshes and matching icons.
- Icon packs with a consistent background and lighting.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Icons rendered with different camera angles.
- Mixing realistic and cartoon items.

docs.title: Building
docs.summary: Placing structures and bases: snapping, stability and upgrades.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can place structures where I want.
- As a player, I can see if a placement is valid before confirming.
- As a player, I can upgrade or remove what I built.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A ghost preview, green when valid and red when not.
- Costs shown before placing.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Structures snap to a grid.
- Removing returns part of the cost.

docs.title: Building System
docs.summary: Snapping, stability checks and how bases are stored.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Building pieces snap to sockets; a stability check walks from the foundation to each piece.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UBuildingPieceComponent`: sockets and stability
- `UBuildingSubsystem`: saves and loads bases

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Piece definitions and costs in data assets.

docs.title: World
docs.summary: The environment the player survives in, and how it changes.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can explore distinct regions.
- As a player, I can find my way back to places I've been.
- As a player, I can notice that the world reacts to what I've done.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- Each region has its own look and landmarks.
- A map that fills in as I explore.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Regions open up as the story progresses.
- Fast travel only between places I've visited.

docs.title: World Generation

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: The world is generated from a seed with biomes placed by temperature and moisture maps.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text: - `UWorldGenerator`: terrain, biomes and points of interest

examples.heading: Data

docs.title: Day and Night
docs.summary: The day/night cycle and weather, and how they change danger.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: A time-of-day system drives the sun, sky and temperature; weather is chosen from a weighted list each day.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UTimeOfDaySubsystem`: clock, sun and temperature
- `UWeatherSubsystem`: weather states and transitions

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Day length and weather weights in data assets.

docs.title: Threats
docs.summary: Creatures and other dangers.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can face creatures that hunt at night.
- As a player, I can hide or fight.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Sounds that warn of a creature nearby.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Creatures are more dangerous at night.
- Fire keeps most creatures away.

docs.title: UI
docs.summary: Menus and HUD: what the player sees and can do outside the game world.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can start, pause and quit from clear menus.
- As a player, I can change graphics, audio and control settings.
- As a player, I can see the information I need during play without it covering the action.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A title screen, pause menu and settings screens.
- A HUD with only what matters right now.
- Button prompts that match my input device.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every screen can be used with a gamepad as well as mouse and keyboard.
- Pausing stops gameplay time.
- Settings save immediately.

docs.title: UI Framework
docs.summary: How screens and widgets are built, opened, navigated and fed data.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Screens are UMG widgets pushed onto a stack by a UI manager subsystem. The top screen gets input; popping it returns to the one below. Gameplay talks to the HUD through events, never directly.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UProjectUISubsystem`: owns the screen stack and opens and closes screens
- `UScreenWidget`: base class for every full screen (menus, settings)
- `UHUDWidget`: the in-game HUD; listens to gameplay events

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Screen classes and their input modes in a data asset.
- Settings in the game user settings, saved per user.

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Clean and readable first: flat shapes, high contrast, one accent color. Icons share one line weight and perspective.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- UI kits with matching icons, buttons and panels.
- Fonts licensed for games, with the character sets we localize to.
- Input prompt packs covering keyboard, Xbox and PlayStation.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Mixing icon packs with different styles.
- Ornate frames that crowd the screen.
- Fonts that are hard to read at small sizes.

examples.text: Music sets the mood of each area; sound effects are short and punchy so they read over the music.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Music packs with loopable stems.
- Sound effect libraries with variations of each sound.
- Licenses that allow commercial use and streaming.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Tracks that don't loop cleanly.
- Effects with long tails that muddy fast moments.
- Mixing many libraries with different loudness.

docs.title: Save and Load
docs.summary: Saving the world, bases and inventory, and keeping saves compatible.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: A save game object holds everything that persists. Systems register what they need saved; saving serializes it to a slot, loading restores it before the level starts. Saves carry a version number so old saves can be migrated.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `USaveSubsystem`: saves and loads slots, runs migrations
- `UProjectSaveGame`: the saved data, with a version field
- `ISaveable`: interface for systems that write and read their part

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Save slots in the platform's save location.
- A version number per save, bumped on every breaking change.
